name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q01 - Match muscle fibres and sarcomere components

questiontext.text:
Match the following and mark the correct option:

Column I Column II
A. Fast muscle fibres i. Myoglobin
B. Slow muscle fibres ii. Lactic acid
C. Actin filament iii. Contractile unit
D. Sarcomere iv. I-band

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Physiological and Structural Characteristics
Fast muscle fibres (white muscle fibres) possess fewer mitochondria and a low concentration of myoglobin. Consequently, they depend primarily on anaerobic glycolysis during strenuous contractions, leading to the accumulation of lactic acid. In contrast, slow muscle fibres (red muscle fibres) are rich in myoglobin and mitochondria, facilitating sustained aerobic ATP production and contraction without rapid fatigue.

Step 2: Myofibrillar Organization
The light isotropic band (I-band) consists predominantly of thin actin filaments. The sarcomere is the segment of a myofibril bounded between two consecutive Z-lines and represents the fundamental functional contractile unit of skeletal muscle.

Step 3: Evaluation of Matches
Fast muscle fibres correspond to lactic acid; slow muscle fibres correspond to myoglobin; actin filament corresponds to the I-band; and sarcomere corresponds to the contractile unit.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct match is A-ii, B-i, C-iv, D-iii.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q02 - Attachment site of human ribs ventrally

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Skeletal Anatomy of the Thoracic Cage
The human rib cage consists of 12 pairs of bicephalic ribs that form a protective enclosure for vital thoracic organs. Each rib attaches dorsally to the thoracic vertebrae of the axial skeleton.

Step 2: Ventral Articulation
Ventrally, the true ribs (the first 7 pairs) attach directly to the flat midline bone known as the sternum with the help of hyaline costal cartilage. Rib pairs 8, 9, and 10 connect indirectly to the sternum through the costal cartilage of the seventh rib, whereas the scapula and clavicle belong to the pectoral girdle and the ilium belongs to the pelvic girdle.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Ribs attach ventrally to the sternum.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q03 - Type of movable joint between atlas axis

questiontext.text: What is the type of movable joint present between the atlas and axis?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structural Classification of Synovial Joints
Synovial joints are characterized by a fluid-filled synovial cavity between articulating bones, allowing varying degrees of movement based on anatomical architecture.

Step 2: Articulation between Atlas and Axis
The first cervical vertebra is the atlas and the second is the axis. The odontoid process (dens) of the axis projects upward to form a pivot around which the ring-like atlas rotates. This atlantoaxial joint permits rotational head movements from side to side.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The movable synovial joint present between the atlas and axis is a pivot joint.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q04 - Location of ATPase enzyme in muscle

questiontext.text: ATPase of the muscle is located in

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Molecular Architecture of Muscle Filaments
Each thick filament is a polymer composed of many monomeric proteins called meromyosins. A meromyosin unit consists of a globular head with a short arm (heavy meromyosin or HMM) and a tail (light meromyosin or LMM).

Step 2: Enzymatic Activity of Myosin
The globular head of the myosin molecule contains an active ATPase enzyme site along with an actin-binding site. In the presence of divalent cations, this myosin ATPase hydrolyzes ATP to ADP and inorganic phosphate, releasing the energy required for cross-bridge movement. Actin, actinin, and the troponin complex do not exhibit ATPase activity.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The ATPase enzyme of muscle is located in myosin.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q05 - Vertebral column group containing intervertebral discs

questiontext.text: Intervertebral disc is found in the vertebral column of

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Nature of Intervertebral Discs
Intervertebral discs are specialized fibrocartilaginous pads positioned between adjacent vertebral bodies. They provide shock absorption, distribute axial loads, and allow slight flexibility of the spinal column.

Step 2: Taxonomic Distribution
The presence of fibrocartilaginous intervertebral discs consisting of a peripheral annulus fibrosus and a central remnant of the notochord called the nucleus pulposus is a distinctive anatomical hallmark of the mammalian vertebral column. In other vertebrate groups such as birds, reptiles, and amphibians, intervertebral articulations differ and lack true mammalian discs.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Intervertebral discs are found in the vertebral column of mammals.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q06 - Sequential order of vertebrae in human spine

questiontext.text: Which one of the following is showing the correct sequential order of vertebrae in the vertebral column of human beings?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Regional Organization of Human Vertebrae
The human vertebral column extends along the dorsal axis from the base of the skull to the pelvis. In an adult, it is composed of 26 serially arranged bones divided into five anatomical regions.

Step 2: Craniocaudal Sequence
Tracing the vertebral column from the cranial end superiorly to the caudal end inferiorly reveals the following order:
1. Cervical region (7 vertebrae in the neck)
2. Thoracic region (12 vertebrae in the chest)
3. Lumbar region (5 vertebrae in the lower back)
4. Sacral region (1 fused bone composed of 5 embryonic vertebrae)
5. Coccygeal region (1 fused bone composed of 4 embryonic vertebrae)

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequential order of vertebrae is cervical — thoracic — lumbar — sacral — coccygeal.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q07 - Incorrect pair of joint and skeletal location

questiontext.text: Which one of the following pairs is incorrect?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Classification of Synovial Joints
Synovial joints are classified by their articulating surfaces and planes of motion. Examples include pivot, hinge, gliding, saddle, and ball-and-socket joints.

Step 2: Evaluation of Joint Pairings
The articulation between the head of the humerus and the glenoid cavity of the pectoral girdle is a multi-axial ball-and-socket joint, not a uniaxial hinge joint. The joint between the atlas and axis is a pivot joint; the joint between adjacent carpal bones is a gliding joint; and the joint between the trapezium (carpal) and first metacarpal of the thumb is a saddle joint.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The incorrect pair is hinge joint: between Humerus and Pectoral girdle.

answer.text: Hinge joint: between Humerus and Pectoral girdle
Saddle joint : between carpals and metacarpals of thumb

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q08 - Joint classification of human knee and elbow

questiontext.text: Knee joint and elbow joint are examples of

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Mechanics of Uniaxial Joints
A hinge joint is a type of synovial joint in which the convex cylindrical surface of one bone fits into the concave depression of another bone, restricting movement to a single plane (flexion and extension).

Step 2: Knee and Elbow Joint Analysis
The elbow joint (between the trochlea of the humerus and the trochlear notch of the ulna) and the knee joint (between the condyles of the femur and the tibial plateau) operate like a door hinge, permitting angular motion primarily along one axis.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Knee joint and elbow joint are examples of hinge joints.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q09 - Type of movement exhibited by leucocytes

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Cellular Movements in the Human Body
Cells in the human body can exhibit three primary types of movement: amoeboid, ciliary, and muscular.

Step 2: Mechanism of Leukocyte Locomotion
Specialized immune cells such as macrophages residing in tissues and white blood cells (leucocytes) circulating in blood move through tissues by extending pseudopodia. This movement is driven by cytoplasmic streaming and the coordinated rearrangement of cytoskeletal microfilaments, enabling them to squeeze through capillary walls (diapedesis) and engulf foreign matter.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Macrophages and leucocytes exhibit amoeboid movement.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q10 - Identification of disorder not affecting bones

questiontext.text: Which one of the following is not a disorder of bone?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Skeletal Disorders
Skeletal system disorders directly involve bones, cartilage, or joints. Arthritis is inflammation of the joints; osteoporosis is characterized by low bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration of bone tissue; and rickets is impaired mineralization of bone matrix during development due to vitamin D or calcium deficiency.

Step 2: Cardiovascular Disorders
Atherosclerosis is a circulatory disease involving the buildup of fibrofatty plaques containing cholesterol, lipids, and fibrous tissue inside the lumina of medium and large arteries, leading to narrowed blood vessels rather than bone pathology.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Atherosclerosis is not a disorder of bone.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q11 - Incorrect statement regarding muscle types and functions

questiontext.text: Which one of the following statement is incorrect?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Classification of Muscle Tissue
Human muscle tissue is categorized into three distinct varieties: skeletal, visceral (smooth), and cardiac muscle.

Step 2: Histological and Functional Properties
Cardiac muscle forms the wall of the heart; its fibers are branched, striated, and involuntary. Skeletal muscles associated with limb bones (hands and legs) are cylindrical, striated, and under voluntary somatic nervous control. Visceral muscles located in hollow internal organs—such as the alimentary canal and reproductive tract—are non-striated (unstriated), spindle-shaped, and under involuntary autonomic regulation.

Step 3: Identification of the Flawed Concept
Describing the muscular tissue lining the alimentary canal as striated is incorrect because visceral organs are lined with unstriated smooth muscle.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The incorrect statement is that the muscles located in the inner walls of alimentary canal are striated and involuntary.

answer.text: The muscles of hands and legs are striated and voluntary
The muscles located in the inner walls of alimentary canal are striated and involuntary
Muscles located in the reproductive tracts are unstriated and involuntary

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q12 - Correct articulation of the head of humerus

questiontext.text: Which one of the following statements is true?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Anatomical Articulations of Girdles
The pectoral girdle consists of two bones: the clavicle and the scapula. The scapula bears a shallow lateral depression known as the glenoid cavity.

Step 2: Shoulder Joint Articulation
The smooth hemispherical head of the humerus articulates with the glenoid cavity of the pectoral girdle to form the multi-axial ball-and-socket shoulder joint. In contrast, the acetabulum is a deep cup-shaped socket located in the pelvic (hip) girdle that articulates with the head of the femur.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The true statement is that head of humerus bone articulates with the glenoid cavity of pectoral girdle.

answer.text: Head of humerus bone articulates with acetabulum of pectoral girdle.
Head of humerus bone articulates with the glenoid cavity of pectoral girdle.
Head of humerus bone articulates with acetabulum of pelvic girdle.
Head of humerus bone articulates with a glenoid cavity of pelvic girdle.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q13 - Characteristics of striated involuntary cardiac muscle tissue

questiontext.text: Muscles with characteristic striations and involuntary are

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structural and Functional Muscle Categories
Muscles are classified structurally as striated or unstriated, and functionally as voluntary or involuntary based on their mechanism of nervous excitation.

Step 2: Comparison Across Locations
Skeletal muscles (such as muscles assisting locomotion and muscles moving the eyelids) possess cross-striations and operate under voluntary control. Visceral smooth muscles (such as muscles in the wall of the alimentary canal) are unstriated and involuntary. Cardiac muscle fibers forming the heart wall contain organized sarcomeres with distinct transverse striations, intercalated discs, and rhythmic autonomic, involuntary contractions.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Muscles that possess striations and function involuntarily are muscles of the heart.

answer.text: Muscles in the wall of alimentary canal

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTIONANDMOVEMENT_MCQ_Q14 - Matching skeletal structures with corresponding anatomical features

questiontext.text:
Match the followings and mark the correct option:

Column I Column II
A. Sternum i. Synovial fluid
B. Glenoid Cavity ii. Vertebrae
C. Freely movable joint iii. Pectoral girdle
D. Cartilaginous joint iv. Flat bones

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structural Anatomy of the Bones
The sternum is a flat bone situated along the anterior midline of the thorax. The glenoid cavity is an articular depression situated on the lateral angle of the scapula, which belongs to the pectoral girdle.

Step 2: Joint Classification and Articulations
Freely movable joints (synovial joints) are distinguished by the presence of a lubricating synovial fluid within the joint cavity. Cartilaginous joints connect articulating bones via cartilage and permit restricted movement, as observed between adjacent vertebrae in the vertebral column.

Step 3: Correlation of Pairs
Sternum pairs with flat bones; glenoid cavity pairs with the pectoral girdle; freely movable joint pairs with synovial fluid; and cartilaginous joint pairs with vertebrae.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct match is A-iv, B-iii, C-i, D-ii.
